case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Bankruptcy Code permits a Chapter 11 plan to impose nonconsensual releases that extinguish creditors’ claims against nondebtor third parties (e.g., the Sacklers) who have not filed for bankruptcy.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Bankruptcy Code Chapter 11 plan-confirmation and discharge framework, principally 11 U.S.C. §§ 105(a), 1123(b), 1129, and 524(e) (and related provisions governing the scope/effect of discharge and plan terms).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The U.S. Trustee argues that the Bankruptcy Code does not authorize bankruptcy courts to approve nonconsensual third-party releases for nondebtors as part of a Chapter 11 plan because (1) the Code’s discharge is a debtor-specific remedy and § 524(e) indicates a debtor’s discharge does not affect others’ liability; (2) general provisions like §§ 105(a) and 1123(b) cannot be used to create a power Congress did not grant—especially a power that effectively grants a bankruptcy-like discharge to nondebtors; (3) allowing such releases rewrites substantive rights of nonconsenting claimants without a clear statutory basis, raising serious due process and structural concerns; and (4) if Congress wanted nondebtor discharges it knew how to provide them (as in the asbestos-specific channeling-injunction regime), so courts should not infer an atextual, sweeping release power.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Purdue (and plan proponents/supporters) defend the releases as permissible plan terms and an appropriate exercise of the bankruptcy court’s equitable and confirmation powers because (1) Chapter 11 is designed to enable comprehensive, global resolutions of mass-tort liabilities and preserve value for victims, and the Sackler contribution was allegedly conditioned on receiving release protection; (2) provisions such as §§ 105(a) and 1123(b), together with the confirmation standards in § 1129, are said to give courts flexibility to approve plan provisions needed to implement reorganization and maximize estate value; (3) many lower courts have allowed nondebtor releases in limited circumstances (e.g., where they are integral to the plan, supported by creditor majorities, and necessary to secure substantial contributions), and the Second Circuit sustained the releases under that body of doctrine; and (4) prohibiting such releases could reduce recoveries, increase litigation, and destabilize existing restructuring practice in mass-tort cases.
key_precedents: Lower-court doctrine permitting/limiting nondebtor third-party releases in Chapter 11 (various circuit approaches, including the Second Circuit decision below)

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Bankruptcy Code permits a Chapter 11 plan to include nonconsensual third-party releases that extinguish creditors’ claims against nondebtors (e.g., owners/affiliates), even though those nondebtors have not filed for bankruptcy.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primarily the Bankruptcy Code—especially 11 U.S.C. § 524(e) (effect of discharge on liabilities of others) and the Chapter 11 plan-confirmation provisions (including 11 U.S.C. §§ 1123, 1129) and the bankruptcy court’s general equitable powers under 11 U.S.C. § 105(a).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The U.S. Trustee argues that the Bankruptcy Code does not authorize bankruptcy courts to impose nonconsensual releases of direct claims that nondebtors hold against other nondebtors; § 524(e) reflects Congress’s choice that a debtor’s discharge does not affect third-party liability, and the Code’s specific, carefully delimited release/injunction mechanisms (and plan-confirmation rules) cannot be expanded via § 105(a) or general plan provisions to grant what functions as a nondebtor discharge without statutory authorization.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Purdue and supporting respondents contend that Chapter 11 permits (at least in extraordinary cases) plan provisions approving third-party releases when they are integral to the reorganization/settlement, overwhelmingly supported by affected creditor constituencies, and necessary to obtain substantial value (here, the Sacklers’ contributions) for victims; they argue the plan and court’s equitable authority can accommodate such releases as part of a global resolution that maximizes recovery and that the Code does not categorically forbid them.
key_precedents: Second Circuit decision affirming confirmation (reported at 69 F.4th 45)
